This research investigates an efficient method for estimating value functions in policy learning, specifically tailored for large-scale control systems with complex dynamics. By leveraging a compact set of samples, we develop an efficient estimate of the value function that minimizes the error, and demonstrate its performance in various scenarios. Notably, we show that this estimate yields a policy that excels in a large subset of samples, even when the sample size is substantial, and that its performance is comparable to the optimal policy in a smaller subset of samples. Additionally, we establish that the error of this estimate decreases proportionally to the square root of the sample size, and that it can be further reduced by increasing the compact set of samples. Furthermore, we apply this efficient estimate to solve complex control problems, including a large-scale multi-agent system and a complex stochastic system, and achieve superior results compared to conventional policy learning methods.

The ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC has obtained a comprehensive dataset of charged particles, pions, kaons, and protons from high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. This study examines the transverse momentum spectra and elliptic flow of identified particles within a broad range of transverse momenta, extending from a few hundred MeV to several hundred GeV. The transverse momentum dependence of the elliptic flow parameter is found to exhibit a similar trend for all identified particles, with the exception of charged hadrons at very low transverse momenta. The study also reveals that the ratio of elliptic flow to entropy density exhibits a particle-independent trend for all identified particles, with the exception of charged hadrons at very low transverse momenta. The transverse momentum dependence of the ratio of elliptic flow to entropy density is found to be consistent with the expectations of viscous hydrodynamics, with a viscosity-to-entropy density ratio of approximately 4-7 times that of the square of the speed of light.

We investigate the performance of binary power control in large interference networks, examining its performance relative to optimal power control. Our analysis reveals that binary power control yields a 2.57 times larger average signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR), and a 3.57 times larger SINR threshold probability, compared to optimal power control. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the performance of binary power control remains comparable to optimal power control in dynamic scenarios.

A new multiple-time-step integration algorithm (MTSA) has been developed to enhance the computational performance of particle-laden flow simulations, particularly in scenarios with a wide range of time scales, as seen in sediment transport and bubble plumes. This algorithm employs a combination of implicit and explicit integration methods to solve the Navier-Stokes equations and the particles' equations of motion, respectively, using different time steps for each. As a result, the algorithm can leverage high-performance computing to achieve significant speedup, with a 3-fold gain in computational efficiency on a single node and a 10-fold gain with a large-scale high-performance computing cluster. Furthermore, the algorithm's accuracy has been validated through comparisons with traditional methods, including the Immersed Boundary Method and the Embedded Boundary Method, in simulations of a single particle settling in a channel flow and a bubble plume in a stratified fluid.

This study investigates the application of feedback control to enhance the precision of a robotic hopping system that navigates a soft, sandy surface. The research focuses on a single-legged robotic hopping system with a lightweight, rigid body and a control system that utilizes a state feedback controller. The system's dynamics are analyzed using a simplified model that accounts for the effects of a soft landing surface. The control strategy is designed to track a desired trajectory, and the system's performance is evaluated using a tracking error metric. The study utilizes a direct method to solve the optimal control problem, and the results are compared to those obtained through linearization techniques. The findings demonstrate that the feedback control system effectively tracks the desired trajectory, and the optimal control approach outperforms the linearization method in terms of tracking error. The research also explores the system's behavior in response to varying surface stiffness and robotic hopping frequency. A quark model is developed to calculate the masses and charge radii of mesons composed of a heavy quark and a light quark. This model is based on a harmonic oscillator potential and a Coulomb interaction, and it uses a three-dimensional harmonic oscillator wave function to describe the quark and light quark dynamics. The approach also accounts for the spin symmetry of the strong interaction and the hyperfine structure of the quark masses. By fitting the model to the masses of the D and Ds mesons, the quark masses and the harmonic oscillator frequency are determined, and the predicted charge radii of D, Ds, B, and Bs mesons are calculated.

We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a probabilistic framework that represents the hierarchical structure of documents and the co-occurrence of topics within them. This model extends the Multivariate Topic Model (MTM) and enables the analysis of complex information networks by automatically identifying topics that span multiple documents. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HDTM in extracting meaningful topics from a hierarchical document network, using a real-world example of a scientific collaboration network. This network consists of 1,500 documents from 500 papers, written by 1,500 authors who collaborated on 500 projects. We compare the performance of HDTM to traditional statistical techniques, such as Multidimensional Scaling and Hierarchical Clustering, in identifying latent topics from this network. Our results show that HDTM outperforms these techniques in extracting coherent topics from the network, and that the topics it extracts are consistent with the network's hierarchical structure.

Quantum annealing has the potential to efficiently solve complex optimization problems by leveraging the power of quantum fluctuations, yet its effectiveness is often limited by the "annealing gap" issue, where the minimum of the energy landscape is not reached due to quantum tunneling. To overcome this challenge, we propose a method to measure the annealing gap using quantum resources, which can be used to optimize quantum annealing protocols. By analyzing the energy landscape of a sample optimization problem, we demonstrate that the annealing gap can be quantified and used to identify the optimal point at which to terminate the annealing process. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be applied to solve a specific type of combinatorial optimization problems, known as the graph isomorphism problem, which has practical applications in fields such as chemistry and computer science. By analyzing the relationship between the annealing gap and the quantum entanglement of the system, we provide a theoretical framework for understanding the interplay between quantum fluctuations and classical optimization.

Theoretical modeling of the electronic structure of the nickelate material (R Nickel Oxide) is crucial for understanding its magnetic and superconducting properties. However, calculating the precise band structure of this material is challenging due to its complex nature. Researchers have employed a simplified method to analyze the energy dispersion of this material, specifically in the (001) direction, by using a local one-dimensional periodic potential. They have applied this approach to calculate the band structure of this material, specifically in the (001) direction, and have compared their results with existing data obtained from angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy. The results of their calculations indicate that the energy dispersion of this material can be accurately described using a local one-dimensional periodic potential, and that the band structure of this material exhibits a local symmetry, which is consistent with the results obtained from angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy.

The presence of a deconfinement phase transition within a polymeric bag model, which is equipped to handle the chiral and deconfinement aspects of QCD, is being used to investigate the properties of quark stars. This study builds upon the bag model's framework by incorporating a first-order phase transition and a critical endpoint in the phase diagram, which is supported by lattice QCD data. Theoretical calculations of the quark star's mass-radius relation are then performed, accounting for the effects of the phase transition's critical endpoint, the surface tension of the bag, and the chiral chemical potential. The results indicate that the phase transition's critical endpoint has a negligible effect on the mass-radius relation, whereas the surface tension and chiral chemical potential do have a significant impact. The study also reveals that the maximum mass of quark stars is influenced by the surface tension and chiral chemical potential, with the surface tension's effect being more pronounced. The calculated mass-radius relations are then compared to those obtained from general relativistic field equations, which are solved using the MIT bag model and the Polyakov loop model. The comparison shows that the surface tension's effect on the mass-radius relation is consistent across both models, whereas the chiral chemical potential's effect is model-dependent. The study's findings are also used to estimate the surface tension's range, which is found to be between 40 and 60 MeV fm^-2.

Quantum metrology involves utilizing highly precise state measurements to accurately determine physical parameters, a process whose precision is capped by the number variance of the state used. A particular state known as the compass state has demonstrated exceptional precision in estimating a specific parameter, known as the detuning, and has been successfully applied in a variety of experiments. However, the compass state's precision is compromised when confronted with a common disturbance known as damping, a problem that has been addressed in theoretical models. This study investigates the compass state's precision when confronted with damping and finds that its precision is significantly reduced, a problem that becomes more severe as the number of particles increases. As a result, the compass state's precision in estimating detuning is limited to a linear proportion as the number of particles grows exponentially. This study also explores alternative states known as the compass-like states that exhibit improved precision in estimating the detuning when confronted with damping, a problem that can be mitigated by adjusting the interaction time between the particles and their environment.

We've developed a comprehensive radiative transfer model that incorporates the effects of dust opacities and radiative cooling in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Our model allows for the simulation of radiative cooling in the outer regions, which is crucial for accurately determining the temperature profiles in these areas. Our research reveals that radiative cooling is less efficient in the outer regions due to the presence of dust, which leads to a more gradual temperature decline. This finding is particularly evident in the outer regions of disks with low levels of turbulence, resulting in a more pronounced temperature gradient. Our model also demonstrates that radiative cooling is more effective in the outer regions when the temperature is higher, leading to a positive feedback loop that accelerates cooling. This, in turn, causes the temperature to drop more rapidly, ultimately resulting in a steeper temperature gradient. Our model's predictions are consistent with observational data from ALMA, providing a more detailed understanding of the temperature profiles in the outer regions of disks.

This study investigates the growth of harmonic functions on a type of manifold that changes over time, specifically one with a shrinking Ricci soliton, and demonstrates a key estimate for these functions.

A dynamic backdoor attack involves manipulating a neural network so that it misbehaves in response to changing input conditions. Implementing such an attack is challenging, particularly in deep learning models, due to their tendency to overfit and the limited access to training data. A dynamic backdoor attack that activates in a specific time frame or in response to specific audio or text inputs poses an additional obstacle. In this research, we introduce a novel dynamic backdoor attack called TimeTriggered Neural Network Attack (TTNNA), which successfully exploits the temporal characteristics of recurrent neural networks to create a time-dependent backdoor effect. Our experiment demonstrates that TTNNA can successfully compromise a network even when the network is trained using a different time frame than the one used for the attack. Furthermore, TTNNA can be applied to a wide range of classification tasks, including those with limited access to training data. Our research also explores the optimal time frame for the backdoor effect and the impact of TTNNA on networks with varying levels of access to training data.

A precise measurement of the ecliptic latitude dependence of the parallax shift caused by the gravitational interaction between the Sun and nearby stars was achieved using Gaia Data Release 2. A statistical analysis of 1.8 million stars with parallactic errors of less than 10% revealed a significant correlation between parallax shift and ecliptic latitude, with a coefficient of 0.013 ± 0.002 mas, which is in line with predictions from general relativity. This finding is particularly significant as it is the first time this effect has been directly observed with high-precision astrometry.

A key challenge in developing intelligent question answering systems lies in effectively incorporating domain-specific knowledge.  A common issue with current knowledge incorporation methods is that they don't account for the semantic meaning of questions, which can limit their performance.  To address this limitation, a new approach is proposed that utilizes a semantic-driven method to incorporate knowledge, taking into consideration the semantic representation of questions.  This approach is demonstrated through the development of a question answering system that utilizes a knowledge base to answer questions about a specific domain.  The system's performance is evaluated using a set of questions, and the results show that it outperforms a baseline system that uses a traditional incorporation method.  Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of the system's performance is conducted to provide insights into its effectiveness.

Calculating the spectra of small molecular cations with a single unbound electron has been challenging due to the vast number of possible transitions, making it difficult to create a full model of their spectrum. This issue arises because the number of possible transitions between energy levels is directly proportional to the square of the number of energy levels, which is infinite in this case. As a result, researchers have traditionally relied on simple theories to predict the energy of individual levels rather than calculating the spectrum directly from a potential energy function. However, these theories often fail to accurately account for the interactions between electrons and the influence of molecular vibrations. In this study, we have developed a new method to calculate the spectrum of small molecular cations with a single unbound electron by combining a simple theory to predict the energy levels and a model of molecular vibrations. This approach has been applied to calculate the spectrum of the N2+ and CO+ molecular cations in their ground state, with the results being in good agreement with experimental measurements.

Distributed machine learning models often rely on a central node to process and aggregate data from multiple nodes, but this can be inefficient due to the need for frequent inter-node communication. To address this limitation, we propose a novel method that leverages random walk algorithms to enable the central node to learn the optimal data routing paths, thereby minimizing unnecessary communication. This approach is particularly effective in scenarios where the underlying graph structure is unknown or dynamic. We also introduce a new algorithm that combines random walk-based routing with gradient descent to optimize model performance, and demonstrate its effectiveness in various real-world applications, including image classification, natural language processing, and recommendation systems.

A significant body of research has shown that providing mental health treatment to offenders can lead to a decrease in their likelihood of committing crimes in the future. However, the majority of this research has focused on the effectiveness of mental health interventions within the prison system, leaving a knowledge gap regarding the impact of pre-sentence mental health treatment on post-release recidivism. This study aims to address this void by examining the relationship between pre-sentence mental health treatment and post-release recidivism among offenders who have committed violent crimes. A comprehensive review of relevant studies was conducted, and the findings were used to develop a statistical model to assess the effect of pre-sentence mental health treatment on post-release recidivism among violent offenders. The results of this study suggest that pre-sentence mental health treatment has a positive effect on reducing violent offenders' likelihood of committing crimes in the future, with the most significant reductions observed in property-related crimes and violent crimes. Furthermore, the study found that the effectiveness of mental health treatment is influenced by the type of crime committed, with offenders who committed violent crimes experiencing a greater decrease in recidivism rates than those who committed property-related crimes.

In the context of medical image segmentation under partial supervision, our novel approach employs a straightforward yet effective method to combine unlabeled images, leveraging a simple interpolation-based mixing technique that applies a regularizing effect. This strategy, which we call semi-supervised re-weighted ensemble segmentation, or SSRWS, is designed to produce a reliable, pseudo-labeled dataset for training. By incorporating unlabeled images and their corresponding pseudo-labels, SSRWS generates a diverse set of pseudo-labeled images that can be used as additional supervised data. We then employ an ensemble learning framework to combine the pseudo-labels and the original labeled data, using re-weighting to prioritize the most accurate predictions. Our method is versatile and can be applied to various ensemble techniques, including voting and weighted combination. We have tested SSRWS on two distinct medical image segmentation tasks: the segmentation of cardiac left ventricle from MRI scans and the segmentation of tumor from pancreatic MRI scans. Our results demonstrate that SSRWS yields superior performance when compared to other semi-supervised learning methods, including the use of adversarial neural networks and consistency training.

We introduce a novel graph neural network-based method to calculate local atomic environments in materials, which we call GNET-LE, short for Graph Neural Network Environment Tracker-Local Environment. This approach identifies and quantifies unique local atomic configurations within materials using a graph neural network, and we demonstrate GNET-LE's effectiveness in accurately predicting local atomic environments in materials using simulated data and experimental data from X-ray scattering. Furthermore, GNET-LE is applied to predict local atomic environments in materials using X-ray absorption near edge structure spectra, and the results show that this method can be used to analyze materials with complex structures.

We establish the weak convergence of the normalized sequence of functionals of the empirical process under the condition that the original sequence converges weakly, without requiring the law of large numbers as an additional premise. This achievement is a direct outcome of our main theorem, which provides a weak convergence criterion for the functional of the empirical process. This criterion is characterized by the weak convergence of the original sequence under the condition that the functional of the sequence converges to a specific value, and it serves as a significant extension of the existing results on the weak convergence of functionals of the empirical process.

Knowledge tracing is a crucial task in educational technology, and deep learning methods have been widely applied to achieve high accuracy. However, evaluating these methods is challenging due to the lack of large-scale student data. To address this issue, we propose a novel method to leverage the knowledge of students who have completed similar courses, enabling the evaluation of deep learning knowledge tracing models using a small-scale student dataset. We also introduce a new dataset, consisting of 1,000 students who have completed 2,000 courses, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in evaluating deep learning knowledge tracing models by comparing them to conventional evaluation methods. Our results show that the proposed method yields consistent evaluation outcomes, whereas the conventional method yields inconsistent results, especially when using small-scale student data.

We establish a key result regarding the surjectivity of second-order elliptic differential operators within a well-defined function space, specifically in the context of smooth functions on a smooth manifold without boundary. Our proof involves demonstrating the existence of a bounded inverse operator for a particular class of differential operators, which in turn enables us to prove the desired surjectivity property. Ultimately, this leads to a significant improvement in the conditions required for the surjectivity of these differential operators, surpassing the previously established standards.

In 2019, veriT's proof format was first presented at the PxTP workshop, and since then, the format has undergone significant changes. This paper outlines the evolution of the veriT proof format, highlighting its development from a basic structure to a sophisticated system capable of representing various mathematical concepts and logical relationships. The proof format's growth is reflected in the increasing complexity of its syntax and semantics, as well as the addition of features to address limitations and user feedback. The paper also examines the format's applications, including its use in theorem provers, automated reasoning tools, and educational platforms.

A novel federated learning algorithm called FedBuff has been developed to address the challenges of large-scale and privacy-sensitive settings. FedBuff introduces a hierarchical framework that divides data into multiple layers, enabling the creation of multiple, smaller datasets from a single large dataset. This approach allows for the creation of multiple, independent datasets that can be used in parallel, thereby significantly enhancing the scalability of the algorithm. Additionally, FedBuff incorporates a hierarchical mechanism to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive data, thereby maintaining the privacy of the data. A theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence properties has been conducted, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated through numerical simulations in various settings.

Speech recognition systems have achieved significant improvements with the advent of deep learning, yet they struggle to adapt to languages with minimal training data. This study investigates the effectiveness of transfer learning in speech recognition for languages with low similarity, using a prototype of the Wombo Knowledge Speech Recognition System. We conducted experiments using a dataset of 20 languages with varying levels of similarity to English, and found that transfer learning is highly effective, even when the target language has little relation to the source language. Specifically, we found that a pre-trained model can achieve 20% to 50% better results when applied to a language with some similarity, and up to 80% better results when applied to a language with little similarity. This is particularly evident when comparing the results for Japanese and Korean, which show that transfer learning can achieve 30% to 50% better results when applied to these languages. This research demonstrates the potential of transfer learning in speech recognition for languages with low similarity, and highlights the importance of developing pre-trained models that can adapt to new languages with minimal training data.

We develop a novel, efficient method called SPGP-SARSA for policy evaluation in underwater navigation, leveraging a Gaussian process to represent the value function and an approximate dynamic programming approach to optimize policy performance. By applying this approach, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of policy evaluation, making it an attractive solution for large-scale underwater navigation applications. In our study, we utilize a Gaussian process to model the value function, and an approximate dynamic programming framework to optimize policy performance. We then derive an iterative update rule for the value function, and demonstrate that this method converges to the optimal solution. Furthermore, we develop a practical algorithm based on this framework, and evaluate its performance in a simulated underwater navigation scenario. The results of this evaluation indicate that SPGP-SARSA significantly outperforms existing methods for policy evaluation in underwater navigation.

We derive a general method to obtain solutions for relativistic stellar models with two fluids from those with a single fluid, under the assumption that the fluid components move in the same direction and have a common four-velocity. This approach is applied to create two-fluid models of rotating anisotropic stars from their isotropic counterparts. Specifically, we use the Weyl semilinear formalism to derive the anisotropic star equations from their isotropic versions, and then use the Einstein field equations to obtain the two-fluid equations of state. Ultimately, we use these derivations to create two-fluid models of rotating anisotropic stars from their isotropic counterparts, and compare the properties of these models to each other and to the original anisotropic star solutions.

To enhance the performance of neural machine translation models, a technique called gradient-entropy regularization control (GEC) has been employed, which involves training models to produce translations with controlled entropy. However, the lack of pre-trained GEC models limits their widespread use. To address this challenge, we developed an adaptation method to convert existing neural machine translation models, which were trained on a different task, into GEC models. Our approach builds upon the concept of multi-task transfer learning, where we fine-tune the pre-trained models on a small GEC dataset. Our proposed adaptation method surpasses this traditional approach in a controlled experiment, where we adapted a large-scale neural machine translation model to a smaller GEC task. Our results indicate that our method yields a GEC model with a higher BLEU score compared to the baseline transfer learning approach.

The concept of fair allocation of divisible goods among multiple agents has been extensively studied under different constraints and assumptions. In the context of divisible goods and multiple agents, the Round-Robin mechanism is a straightforward and efficient fair allocation method that has been proven to yield allocations with high efficiency. However, determining whether the Round-Robin mechanism yields allocations that are at least as efficient as those derived from the cut-and-choose algorithm under the constraint of identical agent values is a challenging problem. In this study, we develop a new approach to compare the efficiency of allocations obtained through the Round-Robin mechanism and the cut-and-choose algorithm. We demonstrate that this comparison yields a specific system of equations with non-negative coefficients, which can be solved to determine if the Round-Robin mechanism yields allocations that are at least as efficient as those obtained from the cut-and-choose algorithm under the constraint of identical agent values. Furthermore, we establish that this system of equations can be solved in a polynomial time, which enables us to determine if the Round-Robin mechanism yields allocations that are at least as efficient as those derived from the cut-and-choose algorithm under the constraint of identical agent values in a polynomial time.

UGC 8839, a spiral galaxy with a low stellar mass, exhibits a unique HII region population, with a significant number of HII regions located in the outer regions of the disk. This is particularly striking when compared to other spiral galaxies of similar mass, which typically have HII regions concentrated in the inner regions. We investigated this phenomenon by conducting a comprehensive study of UGC 8839's HII region population, utilizing a combination of H-alpha imaging and optical spectroscopy. Our analysis revealed that the outer regions of UGC 8839 harbor a substantial number of HII regions, with a peak in the radii range of 4.5 to 6.5 kpc. This is a notable departure from the standard spiral galaxy HII region distribution, which typically peaks in the inner regions. We propose that the unusual distribution of HII regions in UGC 8839 may be attributed to the presence of a massive young star-forming disk, which is fueled by gas and dark matter. This disk is thought to be responsible for the observed HII region population in the outer regions, as well as the galaxy's overall rotation curve and the presence of a central stellar mass deficit.

Using lattice QCD at the physical light quark mass, we have calculated the masses of the pion, the kaon, and the proton in a wide range of quark mass ratios, where the masses of two quark flavors are different, and the third is a variable mass. This was done by applying the method of analytic continuation to data previously calculated in simulations with six different quark masses. Our results show that the mass of the pion is directly proportional to the square root of the product of the masses of the two lighter quarks, and its decay constant is proportional to the product of those masses. Furthermore, we have found that the mass of the kaon is directly proportional to the sum of the masses of the strange and light quarks, and its decay constant is proportional to the product of those masses. Our calculations also show that the mass of the proton is directly proportional to the product of the masses of the strange and light quarks, and its decay constant is proportional to the product of those masses.

We present the discovery of a highly variable classical T Tauri star, AB Pic, whose spectral type has been reclassified from K7 to M0 based on near-infrared spectra. The star's luminosity has been found to be 1.5 times that of the T Tauri threshold, and its mass and age are estimated to be 0.8 solar masses and 2-4 million years, respectively. AB Pic exhibits significant variability in its H-alpha and U-band light curves, with a peak-to-peak amplitude of 2.5. The star's accretion rate has been found to be extremely high, with a rate of 10 to the power -7 solar masses per year, based on the detection of P-Cygni profiles in its spectra. The star's behavior is consistent with the magnetospheric accretion model, and its high variability is attributed to the presence of a massive circumstellar disk. The star's position in the mass-accretion versus mass-stellar diagrams suggests that it may be experiencing a period of enhanced accretion, which could be a critical phase in its evolution. The star's discovery is significant because it challenges the current understanding of disk evolution in classical T Tauri stars, which suggests that they should experience a steady decline in accretion rates over time.

Offline learning in complex systems with multiple interacting agents poses a significant challenge due to limited access to current data. To address this challenge, a novel Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework is proposed, which represents the system as a combination of individual trajectories shared among agents. This framework enables the offline learning of complex systems by leveraging historical interaction data. In particular, a method is developed to train a neural network that predicts the shared trajectories, which can then be used to train a policy network offline. The effectiveness of the SIT framework is demonstrated through offline learning in complex multi-agent systems, including a challenging soccer game scenario.

Convolutional neural networks have been successfully applied to various tasks in medical imaging, yet their potential for improving image registration remains an area of ongoing research. In our study, we developed a CNN-based method to enhance the performance of non-rigid image registration, specifically for MR-to-MR and MR-to-CT brain images. We modified the standard convolutional neural network architecture to accommodate the complex transformations involved in non-rigid registration, resulting in a U-Net variant with a convolutional layer that accounts for spatial transformations. Our approach leverages a novel loss function that combines intensity-based similarity metrics with a spatial consistency term to ensure the smoothness of transformation maps. We tested our method on a publicly available dataset and compared its performance to conventional intensity-based registration techniques, observing significant improvements in both Dice similarity coefficient and surface distance metrics. Our results demonstrate that CNN-based approach can enhance the performance of non-rigid image registration, yielding a 3.5% increase in Dice similarity coefficient and a 2.5 mm reduction in surface distance compared to conventional intensity-based registration methods.

Quantum systems with multiple particles can exhibit complex nonlocal behavior, and understanding this requires examining the relationships between their individual parts. In multi-particle systems, single-particle entanglement plays a significant role in nonlocal effects and steering, and our research focuses on analyzing these connections. We investigate how single-particle entanglement contributes to nonlocality and steering in both general and specific scenarios, including a particular system consisting of two coupled cavities. Our study also explores the relationship between single-particle entanglement and the system's energy, revealing that it is directly related to the average value of a specific entanglement-related operator. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which single-particle entanglement leads to nonlocal effects and steering, and our findings are supported by explicit calculations for a two-cavity system.

The rapid development of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) systems has led to significant security and privacy risks due to the vast amount of sensitive data being shared. To address this challenge, a Blockchain-based data sharing scheme is proposed for IoV systems. This scheme prioritizes secure and private data sharing by utilizing a multi-authority Identity-Based Cryptosystem (IBCS) and a Blockchain-based incentive mechanism. It ensures the confidentiality and integrity of data by utilizing a homomorphic attribute-based encryption (HABE) protocol and a zero-knowledge proof (ZKP) system. Furthermore, it prevents malicious nodes from manipulating data by utilizing a smart contract-based verification process. The proposed scheme is scalable and efficient due to the use of a multi-authority IBCS and a lightweight incentive mechanism. Theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate the security, efficiency, and effectiveness of the proposed scheme.

V392 Persei, a recurring nova in the constellation Perseus, has been observed exhibiting a nova-like behavior, with a significant eruption occurring in 2013 that was 1.5 times more powerful than its initial 1919 outburst. Researchers used data from the Kepler space telescope to study the binary system's orbital period and the impact of its 2013 eruption on its accretion state. By analyzing the star's brightness variations, they determined the orbital period to be 0.996 days and the duration of its eruption to be approximately 20 days. The team also found that the 2013 eruption caused the system to enter a state of high mass transfer, with the star's mass loss rate increasing to 10 times its pre-eruption rate. This led to a significant decrease in the orbital period by 0.0003 days over the course of a year. V392 Persei's unique behavior provides valuable insights into the binary system's evolution and the effects of a massive eruption on its accretion state.

We propose a novel non-iterative, low-complexity algorithm to determine optimal feedback encoding in a distributed clustering scenario. This approach is specifically designed for a problem where a central controller must direct multiple agents into distinct clusters based on limited feedback from the agents. The algorithm optimizes a cost function that reflects the number of pilots needed to establish each cluster, with the goal of minimizing this cost while adhering to quality-of-service constraints. The proposed solution employs a novel feedback encoding scheme that outperforms traditional Lloyd clustering methods by reducing pilot overhead. The algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated through simulations in a distributed compression scenario and a cellular network, where it achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.

A key challenge in creating robust topological edge states lies in their fragility in the presence of disorder and interactions. Recent studies have demonstrated the robustness of surface currents in both bosonic and fermionic systems, exhibiting topological characteristics even in the presence of strong coupling to an environment. This phenomenon is particularly evident in a specific type of topological system, known as the "hopping dimer model," where robust surface currents persist in the presence of strong disorder and interactions. This paper presents a novel method to simulate surface currents in a fermionic system using a hopping dimer model, which is based on a previous study of a bosonic system. This approach is applied to a specific type of topological system, known as the "Kitaev honeycomb model," which exhibits robust surface currents in its proximate phase. This paper also presents a novel application of the hopping dimer model to simulate the behavior of surface currents in a fermionic system with strong interactions, known as the "Kondo-Jahn-Teller lattice model." This paper presents numerical simulations of surface currents in both the "Kitaev honeycomb model" and the "Kondo-Jahn-Teller lattice model" using a combination of exact diagonalization and dynamical mean-field theory. These simulations demonstrate the robustness of surface currents in both systems, even in the presence of strong interactions and disorder.

This study investigates the asymptotic behavior of the Brans-Dicke theory under a specific initial condition, where a photon escapes to null infinity. The main objective is to determine the condition under which a photon can escape to infinity while scalar gravitational radiation is present. The analysis is conducted within the context of the Brans-Dicke theory, where the asymptotic behavior of the metric is examined in the vicinity of null infinity. The research reveals that a photon can escape to infinity if and only if the asymptotic behavior of the metric satisfies certain decay rates in the vicinity of null infinity. The findings also indicate that the scalar gravitational radiation can be present in the vicinity of null infinity if and only if the asymptotic behavior of the metric meets specific decay rate criteria in the vicinity of null infinity. The study demonstrates that the condition for a photon to escape to infinity is equivalent to the condition for the scalar field to decay at a certain rate in the vicinity of null infinity. The research also presents a global existence and uniqueness result for the Brans-Dicke theory under a specific initial condition, where a photon escapes to null infinity. The analysis is conducted within the context of the Schwarzschild black hole spacetime. The study demonstrates that the condition for a photon to escape to infinity is equivalent to the condition for the scalar field to decay at a certain rate in the vicinity of null infinity. The formation of Population III binary remnants is expected to produce gravitational waves detectable by LISA during the Milky Way's formation. We investigate the distribution of these remnants using a semi-analytical model of galaxy formation and a Monte Carlo simulation of stellar mergers. The merger rate density of Population III binary remnants peaks at a redshift of 7.5, with a rate of 0.2 years inverse per gigaparsec cubed. This rate is primarily driven by the most massive remnants, with masses between 10 and 20 solar masses, and is detectable by LISA.

A novel Stackelberg game theory-based approach is proposed to optimize resource allocation in a multi-cell wireless system to ensure security against a malicious third party. In this scenario, multiple users compete for different resources, and one user, the "leader," has the upper hand and can influence the "followers." To ensure the system's security, the leader allocates resources to the followers in a way that maximizes the system's overall security. The goal of the leader is to allocate sufficient resources to the followers to guarantee the system's security, while the followers aim to maximize their individual benefits. The proposed method takes into account the constraints of limited resources and the varying levels of maliciousness among the followers. To solve this complex problem, a two-stage algorithm is developed, first solving the leader-follower relationships and then applying a descent algorithm to find the optimal solution. The proposed method is tested in a system with multiple cells and varying levels of maliciousness among the users, and the results show that it significantly improves the system's security and efficiency compared to traditional methods.

We've developed a streamlined version of TextWorld, a text-based game designed to assess AI in understanding and generating natural language, with the aim of simplifying the process of conducting large-scale text game experiments. By paring down the original game's complex world state and actions, TextWorldExpress boosts the simulation's throughput while maintaining a high level of difficulty, as evidenced by the comparable performance of top-ranked models on both versions. Our findings also reveal that the most effective models can adapt to the revised game without a significant drop in performance, demonstrating the versatility of these top performers. We've made TextWorldExpress available for use in large-scale text game experiments, with accompanying code and guidelines to facilitate seamless integration into existing workflows.

Deep learning applications have experienced rapid growth in recent years, leading to a significant increase in computational demands and energy consumption. As a result, there is a pressing need to develop high-performance and energy-efficient hardware for deep neural networks. Inspired by the success of hardware-oriented learning, we propose a novel architecture called FDHT-LSTM, which is specifically designed for a particular hardware platform. FDHT-LSTM leverages the properties of a hardware system with a specific memory structure to optimize the performance of a deep neural network. We demonstrate the FDHT-LSTM architecture's effectiveness by applying it to a hardware platform with a memory hierarchy, resulting in a 2.5-fold improvement in throughput and a 3.5-fold reduction in energy consumption compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, we show that FDHT-LSTM can be used to optimize other deep neural networks, including VGG, ResNet, and MobileNet, by modifying its parameters.

We investigate the self-binding energy of a scalar field in anti-de Sitter space, using AdS-critical gravity to validate our calculations. This self-binding energy is a key component in reformulating the Weak Gravity Conjecture, specifically in its AdS-CGC version. By applying the AdS-CGC formulation to a massive scalar field, we derive an expression for its self-binding energy, which is then used to establish a lower bound on the mass-to-charge ratio. This ratio is found to be greater than the negative of the scalar field's self-binding energy, and this inequality is shown to be consistent with the AdS-CGC formulation's mass-charge inequality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the self-binding energy of a massive scalar field in AdS-CGC is non-negative, and this non-negativity is a direct consequence of the AdS-CGC formulation's mass-charge inequality.

We establish a key connection between the zero local cohomology submodule and the characteristic function that determines if a local ring is fractionally rational, thereby extending existing results to a broader class of rings. This involves examining the properties of zero local cohomology submodules in the context of graded rings and their associated graded modules, and demonstrating their invariance under base change. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between zero local cohomology submodules and the characteristic function in the case of graded rings and their associated graded modules, and explore specific examples to illustrate the applicability of these findings.

To address the challenges of integrating renewable energy and managing grid stability, many power systems are adopting redispatch markets that allow for the real-time adjustment of power generation. However, implementing these systems is complex, and their impact on the behavior of power plants and renewable energy sources is not yet fully understood. In this study, we develop a mathematical model to analyze the effects of redispatch markets on the behavior of power plants and renewable energy sources, taking into account the technical limitations of power plants and the uncertainty of renewable energy sources. We also investigate the impact of different market design rules on the behavior of power plants and renewable energy sources, and explore the trade-offs between reducing greenhouse gas emissions and maintaining grid stability. Our results show that the optimal design of the market mechanism can lead to significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, but may also increase the cost of adjusting power generation. We also find that the optimal design of the market mechanism depends on the characteristics of the power plants and renewable energy sources, and that the optimal procurement strategy for the grid operator is influenced by the design of the market mechanism.

This result is applicable to polynomials of a specific degree, which can be expressed as a power of a prime number, and includes a specific condition on the polynomial's irreducibility. The summer season at Saturn's south pole is characterized by a unique polar vortex in the stratosphere, which is distinct from the north polar stratospheric vortex that persists year-round. Contrary to the long-lasting vortex at the north pole, the south polar vortex at Saturn's pole exhibits seasonal behavior, forming in late spring and dissipating in early summer. This study examines the south polar vortex during the summer solstice, utilizing data from the Cassini spacecraft's radio science experiment and a comprehensive atmospheric circulation model. By comparing observations from the north pole, researchers found that the south polar vortex is less stable and has a weaker circulation, which contributes to its seasonal nature. Furthermore, the study reveals that the south polar vortex's instability is linked to the formation of a wave-like disturbance in the atmosphere, which in turn leads to the vortex's breakdown. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the dynamics of Saturn's south polar vortex and its seasonal behavior, shedding light on the complex interactions between the planet's atmospheric circulation and its internal and external energy sources.

We develop a new approach to demonstrate that solutions to the linear Schrödinger equation with a positive potential in a bounded domain will disintegrate over time, even when the solution starts with a compact support inside the domain. Contrary to conventional methods, our approach does not rely on the Carleman estimate, instead, we utilize an integral inequality that assesses the sum of the $L^2$ norms of solutions and their spatial derivatives along a specific time interval, allowing us to draw inferences about the disintegration of solutions in bounded domains with various geometric configurations.

This research paper investigates the interplay between characteristic-zero and positive-characteristic commutative algebra, specifically within the context of graded rings and modules. A primary area of focus is on graded rings and modules exhibiting no negative terms, and with modules also possessing finite generation in each degree. A key concept explored is that of strongly graded modules, which have the property that their degree-$0$ component interacts with the ring's center through a module action that is both commutative and free. A notable result obtained shows that any positive-characteristic strongly graded module with a specific property can be transformed into an equivalent characteristic-zero algebraic structure. A secondary area of study involves the examination of graded modules with a specified property, namely that they are free from the effects of torsion in characteristic zero, and canary properties of graded modules are also discussed.

We introduce the concept of a symplectic double vector bundle as a specific type of symplectic vector bundle that is double, and demonstrate that it is equivalent to a symmetric double vector bundle of rank 2. This definition is further shown to be a subset of the more general definition of a symplectic double vector bundle with a non-degenerate symplectic structure, which includes the case of a symmetric double vector bundle of rank $k$ for any positive integer $k$.

We develop a comprehensive framework for analyzing Lie algebras, focusing on the structure of orbits within the adjoint representation. This framework involves a geometric measure, known as Kirillov's measure, which serves as a key component in our analysis. By examining the properties of Kirillov's measure in relation to the adjoint representation's orbits, we uncover a direct correlation between the measure's multiplicity and the dimension of each orbit. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this measure's multiplicity can be used to categorize Lie algebras into distinct classes, providing a novel and insightful perspective on their underlying structure.

A novel phase retrieval algorithm has been developed to reconstruct energy spectra from x-ray scattering data across multiple energies. This algorithm overcomes the limitations of existing methods by allowing for the simultaneous retrieval of complex wavefields at different energies and their corresponding spectra. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations demonstrate that this new approach yields more accurate reconstructions of energy spectra compared to current methods. Furthermore, this algorithm can be seamlessly integrated with state-of-the-art optimization techniques, such as the difference map algorithm, to yield superior results in phase retrieval and spectrum reconstruction. The effectiveness of this algorithm has been validated through simulations of a realistic experiment involving a complex sample, and it is anticipated that this algorithm will be particularly beneficial for the analysis of x-ray scattering data obtained from synchrotron radiation and free-electron lasers.

We introduce a new mixed finite element method for solving a model problem of multiple blocking fractures in porous media, which is based on a hybrid Darcy-steam flow model. This method involves a hybrid formulation to account for the blocking fractures, and it utilizes a specific mixed finite element approach to solve the Darcy and steam flow equations. The Dirac-$\beta$ function approach is used to model the blocking fractures, and this approach is shown to be equivalent to the standard Beavers-Joseph-Saffman interface condition. The convergence of this method is proven under the assumption of small time steps, and numerical results are provided to demonstrate its effectiveness.

We introduce a novel framework for selecting among multiple hypotheses that is grounded in decision theory. This approach enables the use of utility functions in decision-making, which are a key aspect of the hypotheses themselves. By assigning probabilities to each hypothesis, we can determine expected utility and choose the hypothesis with the highest value. This decision-making process is then used to calculate the expected utility of a given action, which in turn allows us to calculate the expected outcome of that action. This framework is particularly useful in situations where there are multiple possible actions to choose from, as it enables us to select the action with the highest expected outcome.

We present DiscSense, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 2,500 sentences, annotated for the relationship between a word and the discourse marker preceding it, which was created using a multi-step process to ensure accuracy. This dataset stands out from existing resources as it focuses on the connection between words and discourse markers, rather than simply identifying the markers themselves. We demonstrate the utility of DiscSense by training a model to predict the semantic relationship between a word and its preceding discourse marker, which can be a valuable tool in natural language processing tasks such as text classification and sentiment analysis. Our research also explores the relationship between discourse markers and semantic relations, revealing that certain markers are more likely to be associated with specific relations, and that these relations can be influenced by the context in which the sentence is used.

We investigate the geometric characteristics of a simplified version of a complex objective function, referred to as the factorized objective, which is relevant to various matrix optimization problems. Under the assumptions of strong convexity and smoothness of the original objective function, we establish that the factorized objective exhibits strong convexity and smoothness within a specific, restricted domain. This domain is defined by the geodesic distance between the current estimate and the optimal solution, and we demonstrate that this geodesic distance is limited in order to guarantee the desired properties of the factorized objective. We also show that the factorized objective exhibits the property of being strictly convex along geodesic trajectories. These findings are particularly significant in the context of matrix optimization problems, where the factorized objective is commonly used in proximal gradient methods.

In 1990, the problem of determining whether bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 could be strongly edge-colored using just 6 colors was identified as an open question by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza. In 2019, this problem was solved by independently discovering that bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 can be strongly edge-colored using 6 colors by Jooyandeh, Kral', Hager, and Schmit, and also by independently discovering this same result by Chan, Hager, and Schmit.

This study investigates the performance of co-evolutionary genetic algorithms (CGAs) under different learning strategies, focusing on the learning behavior and expected Hamming distance from the Nash Equilibrium (NE) in the Prisoner's Dilemma game. A CGA model was developed to examine the impact of individual and social learning on performance, using a simple GA as the problem-solving component. The results show that social learning leads to better performance and a shorter path to the NE compared to individual learning. Furthermore, the expected Hamming distance from the NE differs significantly between social and individual learning, with social learning resulting in a much shorter distance. The study also found that the expected Hamming distance from the NE is inversely proportional to the learning coefficient in both individual and social learning scenarios.

We investigate the properties of edge ideals in weighted oriented graphs, specifically examining the relationship between their ordinary and symbolic power structures. Our primary objective is to establish the equality between these power structures for all degrees, and we achieve this for specific cases of oriented graphs, including rooted trees, planar quadrangulations, and cubic graphs. Additionally, we derive formulas for the symbolic and ordinary powers of edge ideals in these instances.

Neural networks are highly susceptible to data corruptions, which can significantly compromise their performance and accuracy. To mitigate this issue, researchers have proposed various techniques, including input range restriction methods, to prevent silent data corruptions. These methods limit the input range to a specific domain where the network's behavior remains reliable and free from corruption. However, existing approaches restrict the input range uniformly, which may not be optimal in many cases. In contrast, non-uniform range restriction techniques can better capture the intricate relationships between inputs and network outputs by defining different ranges for different input dimensions. In this research, we introduce a novel non-uniform range restriction technique, which is based on the principle of minimizing the maximum absolute output change when input data is corrupted. We also present a practical method to approximate this technique using a second-order cone program. Furthermore, we propose a data corruption prevention framework that incorporates non-uniform range restriction into the network's training process. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conducted experiments on multiple neural network models and datasets, which demonstrate the superior performance of non-uniform range restriction over existing uniform techniques.

We introduce a generalized version of the Jordanian twist, which is shown to be equivalent to the simple Jordanian twist after a specific redefinition of the underlying algebra. This generalization allows us to extend the original twist construction to more complex situations, specifically to N-dimensional space-time. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of this generalized twist to the U(N) irreducible representation of the Gl(N) algebra, resulting in a star product that can be expressed in terms of the Faddeev-Levezier metric tensor.

We propose a novel method to enhance the effectiveness of sequence tagging in under-resourced languages by leveraging the structural similarity between these languages and a related, better-resourced language. This approach is particularly beneficial for languages without pre-existing annotated data, where traditional supervised learning falls short. Our primary application is to develop a name tagging system for these languages. In our experiments using the Serbian language as an example of a resourced language and Montenegrin as an example of an under-resourced language, our proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art transfer learning techniques by a significant margin, achieving an F-score of 88.5% on the Montenegrin language, which has limited annotated data.

The ALICE experiment at the CERN LHC probed the production of charged particles in various collision systems at the highest energy to date. By examining the ratios of specific particle combinations, researchers discovered a consistent trend across different collision types, including proton-proton, X-ray-produced ion collisions, and the most energetic ion collisions to date. These findings indicate that the same underlying physics principles govern particle production in both small and large-scale collisions. Additionally, the discovery of a consistent pattern in particle ratios in the most energetic ion collisions to date provides a foundation for further exploration of the properties of quark-gluon plasma in the most energetic collisions to date.

We've developed a mathematical model that integrates the complex infrastructure of a modern city, including its transportation systems and social networks, to simulate the spread of protests and potential outcomes. This model, which is grounded in graph theory and differential equations, is capable of replicating various protest scenarios, including the sudden emergence of protests in a single neighborhood, protests spreading rapidly across the city, and protests being suppressed or fueled by the police. By analyzing the model's dynamics, we've identified key factors that influence the protests' trajectory and their ultimate success or failure, including the speed at which they spread, the police's effectiveness in quelling them, and the impact of isolated protests in different neighborhoods. Furthermore, this model can be used to determine the optimal police strategy in response to a protest, which may involve targeting specific neighborhoods, applying varying levels of force, or engaging in dialogue with protesters. By applying this model to real-world data from New York City, we've demonstrated its practical applications and the accuracy of its predictions.

We develop a symbolic technique to determine if one regular expression is contained within another, leveraging Brzozowski's regular expression transformation to create a reverse operator. This operator enables us to check containment using a decision procedure based on regular expression equational logic, which can be performed symbolically. Our approach also yields a containment-checking algorithm for regular expressions with variables.

Deep learning-based Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) models have demonstrated superior performance in recent years, thanks to the availability of large-scale datasets and advanced deep learning techniques. However, the lack of a unified testing platform has hindered the comparison and evaluation of these models. This paper presents a novel VIO assessment framework that integrates a deep learning-based VIO network with a robust Visual-Inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (VISLM) algorithm to enable the comparison of VIO models under various scenarios. The framework leverages the VISLM algorithm to generate precise ground truth data for VIO system state and sensor data, allowing for the assessment of VIO models in both real and synthetic environments. The paper showcases the effectiveness of this framework by applying it to the evaluation of a state-of-the-art VIO network, the DeepVIO, on a diverse set of datasets, including the TUM, ICL-NUIM, and our newly introduced dataset, the Campus dataset. The results demonstrate the superior performance of the DeepVIO network in comparison to the traditional VIO algorithm DSO-EKF in various real-world and synthetic environments.

The study of non-trivial topological properties in materials has led to the discovery of Weyl semimetals, whose unique features enable the propagation of massless, topologically protected particles called Fermi arcs. Building on this foundation, researchers have expanded the concept to higher-order Weyl semimetals, which exhibit topological characteristics in three-dimensional systems. The unique solvability and a priori error estimates of the method are established under the assumption that the boundary is resolved by the mesh. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method can resolve the boundary singularities of the solution, and we provide a numerical example to verify our theoretical findings.

A new method is proposed to facilitate the creation of a student model that is more efficient and accurate, by leveraging a saliency-based approach to selectively transfer knowledge from a pre-trained, high-capacity teacher model. This approach, which is part of a larger knowledge amalgamation framework, involves training the student model using a combination of the student and teacher models, with the aim of identifying the most critical components of the teacher model that are relevant to the student's task. By focusing on the salient parts of the teacher model, the student model is able to bypass unnecessary information and concentrate on the most important aspects, leading to a significant reduction in the number of parameters required. This method is particularly effective when working with large teacher models, as it enables the student model to adapt to new tasks with minimal additional training, resulting in a substantial improvement in performance.

This research focuses on a particular case of S4 extensions, where the quadratic residue symbol is linked to a specific quadratic field and the Galois representation is associated with a particular elliptic curve.
